honesty: Positive path: 10.0.0.15 spreads ~5.7MB across 11 materially-contributing flows to an external collector (203.0.113.200) — below the burst ceiling, inside the low-and-slow band, >= 5 material flows. Cernity's low_slow_exfil fires; raw Suricata (Arm A) has no signature for a benign-looking distributed trickle, so this is a behavioral-gap detection.

Matched benign control (NOT labelled malicious): the SAME host sends a comparable ~5.7MB to 198.51.100.50 concentrated in ONE bulk transfer + 12 tiny callbacks (a legitimate backup upload). It shares the surface features (external egress, elevated bytes, many connections) but has only 1 material flow, so a correct detector stays silent — the §49.4 materiality feature, not a beacon-specific exclusion. 198.51.100.50 must produce NO exfil finding.

Matched AUTHORIZED control (§59.3 selectivity, NOT labelled malicious): the SAME host sends the SAME distributed low-and-slow shape (11 material flows, ~5.7MB) to 192.0.2.100, an AUTHORIZED destination declared on NDR_EXFIL_ALLOWLIST=192.0.2. for the run. The traffic is byte-for-byte the same predicate-matching shape as the positive; the ONLY difference is authorization context. A correct detector must NOT raise low_slow_exfil for 192.0.2.100 — proving distributed material transfer is not itself proof of malice, selectivity comes from context.
Synthetic, hand-built scenario; a single engineered host is not a prevalence sample. Real precision/recall need a labelled corpus (see CIC-IDS / CTU-13 in registry.json).
caveats: Genuine bytes: MSS-sized TCP segments carry real payload, so Suricata's per-flow bytes_toserver reflects the actual transfer (no jumbo-frame inflation).
Offline replay measures detection + analyst-volume, not throughput.
